hints: Look at what group has been added to benzene to make cumene, which is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, and think what chloroalkane could supply that $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ fragment.
Remember that when $\text{H}$ from the ring is replaced by an alkyl group from $\text{R-Cl}$, the $\text{Cl}$ must leave with that $\text{H}$ as a small inorganic molecule.
walkthrough:
Spot the new side chain**
Cumene is isopropylbenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$. Compared with benzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, one ring $\text{H}$ has been swapped for a $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ group. That three carbon fragment must come from D.

Choose the chloroalkane precursor**
In Friedel-Crafts alkylation the alkyl group is delivered as a chloroalkane, $\text{R-Cl}$. To deliver an isopropyl group you need $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_3$, which is 2-chloropropane. The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond breaks to generate the electrophile.

Balance the leftover atoms**
Benzene loses $\text{H}$ and D loses $\text{Cl}$, so they combine to form $\text{HCl}$. That is the non-organic product E. Equation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2 + \text{HCl}$.

Final answer: D is 2-chloropropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_3$.
E is hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$.

hints: Think of the general name for benzene reacting with a haloalkane in the presence of a halogen carrier to attach an alkyl group to the ring.
walkthrough:
Recognise the reaction family**
You start with benzene and you finish with an alkylbenzene, with $\text{H}$ substituted by alkyl. Any substitution on benzene by an electrophile is electrophilic substitution, and the specific version that puts an alkyl group on using a haloalkane and catalyst is called Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
Final answer: (Friedel-Crafts) alkylation.

hints: Recall which Lewis acid catalysts are used to polarise $\text{Cl}_2$ for electrophilic attack on the benzene ring, as opposed to UV light for the side chain.
walkthrough:
Separate ring from side chain chemistry**
Chlorination in the aromatic ring is electrophilic substitution and needs a catalyst to make $\text{Cl}_2$ electrophilic enough. The classic carriers are anhydrous aluminium chloride, $\text{AlCl}_3$, or iron(III) chloride, $\text{FeCl}_3$. They accept a lone pair from $\text{Cl}_2$ to generate $\text{Cl}^+$ character.
Final answer: $\text{AlCl}_3$ or $\text{FeCl}_3$ (anhydrous halogen carrier).

hints: Remember that an alkyl group such as isopropyl is activating and directs incoming electrophiles to the positions ortho and para to itself.
walkthrough:
Apply the directing effect**
The isopropyl group, $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, is electron donating by induction and hyperconjugation, so it activates the ring and directs ortho and para. Chlorination therefore gives substitution on the ring at the 2-position or the 4-position relative to the side chain, both of formula $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{11}\text{Cl}$. Either structure earns the mark.
Final answer: 2-chloro-isopropylbenzene (ortho isomer) OR 4-chloro-isopropylbenzene (para isomer), $\text{ClC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$.

hints: Think what condition is needed to split $\text{Cl}_2$ into $\text{Cl}$ radicals for attack on the alkane-like side chain rather than the delocalised ring.
walkthrough:
Switch the mechanism**
Attack on the saturated side chain is not electrophilic substitution, it is free radical substitution. $\text{Cl}_2$ needs homolytic fission to $2\text{Cl}^\bullet$. That is achieved photochemically with UV or sunlight, or thermally at high temperature. No $\text{AlCl}_3$ is used here.
Final answer: UV light or sunlight or high temperature, $T > 100^{\circ}\text{C}$.

hints: Look at the two different types of hydrogen on the isopropyl side chain, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, and imagine replacing one $\text{H}$ on the benzylic carbon versus on a methyl group with $\text{Cl}$.
walkthrough:
Chlorinate the side chain only**
Keep the benzene ring untouched and replace one side chain $\text{H}$ by $\text{Cl}$. There are two distinct environments: the single benzylic $\text{H}$ on the carbon joined to the ring, giving $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(Cl)(CH}_3)_2$, and the six equivalent methyl $\text{H}$ atoms, giving $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. Both have formula $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{11}\text{Cl}$.
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(Cl)(CH}_3)_2$ OR $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$.

hints: Recall what hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ does to any alkyl side chain on benzene, however long it is, and what happens to a nitro substituent under those oxidising conditions.
Recall what $\text{H}_2$ with Ni under high pressure does to a $\text{NO}_2$ group and to a benzene ring, contrasting reduction with oxidation.
walkthrough:
Oxidise the side chain completely**
Hot alkaline or acid $\text{KMnO}_4$ is a powerful oxidiser. Any alkylbenzene side chain, including $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, is cleaved and oxidised right back to a $\text{COOH}$ group directly on the ring. The $\text{NO}_2$ group is already highly oxidised and survives, so a nitrocumene gives nitrobenzoic acid, $\text{O}_2\text{NC}_6\text{H}_4\text{COOH}$.

Reduce the nitro group**
$\text{H}_2$ with Ni catalyst is a reducing system. It delivers hydrogen to the $\text{N=O}$ bonds and converts $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$. Under high pressure even the benzene ring can be further hydrogenated, but the key examined change is nitro to amine reduction, the opposite of oxidation.

Final answer: With hot $\text{KMnO}_4\text{(aq)}$: 4-nitrobenzoic acid, $\text{O}_2\text{NC}_6\text{H}_4\text{COOH}$ (side chain oxidised to $\text{COOH}$, $\text{NO}_2$ unchanged).
With $\text{H}_2$ + Ni, high pressure: $\text{NO}_2$ reduced to $\text{NH}_2$ (e.g. amine product, with possible further ring hydrogenation under forcing conditions).

hints: Identify the actual electrophile in nitration formed from $\text{HNO}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ that attacks the benzene pi system.
Think where the first curly arrow starts, from the benzene delocalised electrons, and where it points to form the new $\text{C-N}$ bond.
Picture the positively charged intermediate after attack, with the charge delocalised over five carbons and one $sp^3$ carbon bearing $\text{H}$ and $\text{NO}_2$.
Consider how aromaticity is restored by breaking the $\text{C-H}$ bond at the site of attack and where that pair of electrons goes.
walkthrough:
Name the attacking electrophile**
Nitration uses concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ in concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to make the nitronium ion, $\text{NO}_2^+$. This linear cation is strongly electron deficient and is the species that the electron rich benzene ring attacks. Write it clearly as $\text{NO}_2^+$.

Show the first bond forming step**
Draw a curly arrow starting in the centre of the benzene ring, representing the delocalised pi electrons, and pointing to the $\text{N}$ atom of $\text{NO}_2^+$. This forms a new $\text{C-N}$ bond and breaks the aromaticity, giving a cyclohexadienyl cation, often called the arenium ion or Wheland intermediate.

Draw the intermediate correctly**
Show a benzene ring with one saturated carbon bearing $\text{H}$ and $\text{NO}_2$, and a horseshoe of delocalisation covering the other five carbons with a + charge. The isopropyl group remains attached elsewhere on the ring. This delocalisation is why the intermediate is relatively stable.

Restore aromaticity**
Draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond at the attacked carbon back into the ring to reform the pi system. The $\text{H}$ leaves as $\text{H}^+$, which is removed by $\text{HSO}_4^-$ or water. Aromaticity is regained, which provides the driving force, giving nitrocumene + $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Electrophile is $\text{NO}_2^+$.
Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\text{NO}_2^+$ to form $\text{C-N}$ bond.
Intermediate is arenium ion with positive charge delocalised over 5 carbons (horseshoe).
Curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond back into ring to reform aromatic system + $\text{H}^+$.
